articles.title: Recycled Fabric Bag Market Growth to Accelerate by 2035 Driven by Plastic Bans and Corporate ESG Commitments - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.author: IndexBox
articles.content:
Freitag
Pioneer in upcycled fabric bags
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Recycled Fabric Bag market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global recycled fabric bag market is undergoing a structural transformation as regulatory pressure, corporate sustainability targets, and shifting consumer preferences converge to reshape demand patterns. By 2035, the market is expected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.2%, with the market index reaching 195 relative to 2025. This growth is underpinned by the bifurcation of the market into a high-volume, low-margin commodity segment—dominated by private-label grocery and promotional bags—and a premium, benefit-led segment where brand narrative, verified recycled content, and design innovation command higher margins. The commodity segment faces intense price competition and margin compression, while the premium segment leverages direct-to-consumer channels and specialty retail to capture value. Supply chain transparency and the integrity of recycled content claims have become primary competitive battlegrounds, with brands unable to substantiate environmental credentials facing regulatory and reputational risk. Geographic roles are sharply defined: North America and Western Europe drive premiumization and brand innovation; manufacturing is concentrated in low-cost Asian hubs with growing domestic demand; and emerging markets present a dual opportunity for low-cost commodity imports and nascent premium local brands. The pricing architecture is fragmented, with deep-discount promotional prices at mass retail eroding perceived base value, while artisanal and designer-branded bags achieve luxury-like price points based on narrative, craftsmanship, and exclusivity. Retailer strategy directly shapes category dynamics, with grocers using private-label bags as low-margin traffic builders and sustainability halo products, while fashion and lifestyle retail
The baseline scenario for the recycled fabric bag market from 2026 to 2035 assumes steady macroeconomic growth, continued regulatory tightening on single-use plastics across major economies, and incremental adoption of circular economy frameworks by retailers and brand owners. Under this scenario, global demand is projected to grow at a CAGR of 7.2%, with the market index reaching 195 by 2035 (2025=100). The market is expected to reach a value of approximately USD 12.8 billion by 2035, up from an estimated USD 6.5 billion in 2025. Volume growth will be driven by substitution of virgin plastic bags in grocery and retail applications, while value growth will be supported by premiumization in fashion and corporate gifting segments. Key assumptions include: (1) the European Union's Single-Use Plastics Directive and similar legislation in North America and Asia-Pacific will continue to phase out lightweight plastic carrier bags, creating a structural demand shift toward reusable and recycled fabric alternatives; (2) corporate ESG commitments will sustain demand for branded promotional bags with verified recycled content; (3) technological improvements in fiber sorting and recycling will increase the availability and quality of recycled polyester and cotton feedstocks, reducing cost premiums; (4) consumer willingness to pay a premium for sustainable products will remain resilient in high-income markets but will be constrained by cost-of-living pressures in the near term; (5) supply chain investments in traceability systems (e.g., blockchain, digital product passports) will become standard, enabling brands to substantiate claims and command price premiums. Risks to the baseline include potential economic slowdowns that could depress promotional spending, volatility in recycled
Retail shopping remains the largest end-use segment for recycled fabric bags, accounting for 35% of global demand. This segment is dominated by reusable grocery and shopping totes, often distributed as private-label items by supermarkets and mass retailers. The mechanism is straightforward: as plastic bag bans and fees proliferate, consumers are compelled to purchase or bring reusable alternatives. Retailers use these bags as low-margin traffic builders and sustainability halo products, often selling them at cost or near cost. Through 2035, demand will be sustained by continued regulatory expansion in Asia-Pacific and Latin America, where plastic bag bans are still being implemented. However, volume growth will moderate as saturation sets in mature markets. The key demand-side indicator is the number of plastic bag bans enacted annually. Value growth will be limited by intense price competition and the commoditization of basic totes. Major trends include the shift toward multi-pack purchases, integration of RFID tags for loyalty programs, and the use of recycled ocean plastic as a premium differentiator. Current trend: Stable growth driven by regulatory substitution and retailer programs.
Major trends: Plastic bag bans expanding to new geographies, particularly in Southeast Asia and Africa, Retailers launching multi-pack reusable bag programs to increase per-customer volume, Integration of digital features such as RFID tags for loyalty and traceability, and Use of ocean-bound recycled plastics as a premium material story.
Representative participants: Walmart Inc, Target Corporation, Carrefour SA, Tesco PLC, Aldi Einkauf GmbH & Co. oHG, and Lidl Stiftung & Co. KG.
Promotional and corporate gifting represents 25% of the market, driven by companies using branded recycled fabric bags as giveaways at trade shows, events, and as part of employee or client gift packages. The mechanism is tied to corporate marketing budgets and ESG reporting: companies seek tangible, visible items that communicate sustainability commitments. Demand is sensitive to economic cycles, as promotional spending is often cut during downturns. Through 2035, growth will be supported by the increasing integration of sustainability metrics into corporate procurement guidelines, with many firms mandating a minimum recycled content percentage for all promotional merchandise. The key demand-side indicator is corporate marketing expenditure on sustainable merchandise. Value growth will outpace volume growth as brands opt for higher-quality, design-forward bags that can be reused and thus provide longer brand exposure. Major trends include the shift toward digital product passports to verify recycled content, customization through direct-to-garment printing, and the use of upcycled fabric pouches for premium gift sets. Current trend: Moderate growth supported by ESG-linked marketing spend.
Major trends: Corporate procurement policies mandating minimum recycled content for promotional items, Shift toward higher-quality, reusable bags to extend brand exposure duration, Adoption of digital product passports for verified sustainability claims, and Growth of upcycled fabric pouches for premium corporate gift sets.
Representative participants: 4imprint Group plc, BIC Graphic, Polyconcept North America, Swag.com (a Vistaprint company), Custom Ink LLC, and Branded Bills LLC.
The grocery and produce segment accounts for 20% of demand, encompassing reusable produce bags, mesh bags, and lightweight shopping bags used for fruits, vegetables, and bulk items. This segment is distinct from general retail shopping bags due to specific functional requirements: bags must be lightweight, breathable, and often transparent for checkout visibility. The mechanism is driven by regulations targeting lightweight plastic produce bags, which are increasingly being banned or taxed in Europe and North America. Through 2035, demand will grow as more jurisdictions extend plastic bag bans to include produce bags, and as consumers form habits of bringing reusable produce bags. The key demand-side indicator is the number of jurisdictions banning lightweight plastic produce bags. Volume growth will be strong but value growth will be constrained by low unit prices and competition from compostable alternatives. Major trends include the development of lightweight recycled polyester mesh bags, integration of tare weight labels for checkout efficiency, and retailer-led programs offering free or subsidized produce bags to customers. Current trend: Steady growth from regulatory substitution and consumer habit formation.
Major trends: Extension of plastic bag bans to include lightweight produce bags in Europe and North America, Development of lightweight recycled polyester mesh bags with tare weight labels, Retailer-led programs offering free or subsidized reusable produce bags, and Competition from compostable bioplastic produce bags in some markets.
Representative participants: Whole Foods Market (Amazon), Kroger Co, Ahold Delhaize, Sainsbury's, Waitrose & Partners, and Marks and Spencer Group plc.
Fashion and accessories represent 12% of the market but command a disproportionate share of value due to higher unit prices and margins. This segment includes designer tote bags, backpacks, crossbody bags, and clutches made from recycled fabrics, often positioned as sustainable luxury or eco-conscious lifestyle products. The mechanism is driven by consumer willingness to pay a premium for products that align with personal values and signal environmental awareness. Through 2035, this segment will grow faster than the market average, supported by the entry of luxury brands into sustainable materials and the rise of direct-to-consumer brands built entirely on recycled narratives. The key demand-side indicator is the share of new product launches featuring recycled content in the fashion accessories category. Value growth will be strong as brands invest in design, craftsmanship, and storytelling to justify higher price points. Major trends include the use of recycled ocean plastics for premium collections, collaborations between fashion houses and recycling technology companies, and the adoption of circular business models such as take-back and repair programs. Current trend: High growth from premiumization and sustainability-driven brand positioning.
Major trends: Luxury brands launching collections using recycled ocean plastics and post-consumer textiles, Direct-to-consumer brands built entirely on recycled fabric narratives, Collaborations between fashion houses and recycling technology firms, and Adoption of take-back and repair programs to extend product lifecycle.

The logistics and packaging segment accounts for 8% of demand, encompassing woven polypropylene sacks, bulk bags, and industrial totes made from recycled fabrics used for transporting and storing goods such as grains, fertilizers, construction materials, and e-commerce returns. The mechanism is driven by cost savings and corporate sustainability goals: recycled fabric sacks are often cheaper than virgin alternatives and help companies meet recycled content targets. Domestic demand is rising as plastic bag bans expand in countries like India, Thailand, and Indonesia. The region also benefits from growing textile recycling infrastructure and government support for circular economy initiatives. Direction: dominant manufacturing hub with growing domestic consumption.
North America is a key market for premium recycled fabric bags, with strong consumer demand for sustainable products and corporate ESG commitments. Plastic bag bans in states like California, New York, and Hawaii are expanding, while federal procurement policies favor recycled content. Value growth outpaces volume as brands invest in design and traceability. Direction: premiumization and regulatory push driving value growth.
Europe remains a regulatory leader with the EU Single-Use Plastics Directive and extended producer responsibility schemes. The market is mature, with high penetration of reusable bags. Growth is driven by premiumization, circular business models, and demand for verified recycled content. Germany, France, and the UK are the largest national markets. Direction: mature market with stringent regulations and high sustainability awareness.
Latin America is experiencing rapid adoption of plastic bag bans, particularly in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Argentina. Domestic manufacturing is limited, leading to reliance on imports from Asia. Growth is driven by regulatory compliance and rising environmental awareness among urban consumers. Value growth is constrained by price sensitivity. The Middle East and Africa represent a small but growing market, with plastic bag bans implemented in countries like Kenya, Rwanda, Morocco, and South Africa. Demand is primarily for low-cost commodity bags. Growth is supported by urbanization, retail expansion, and international development programs promoting sustainable alternatives. Infrastructure constraints limit domestic production. Direction: nascent market with potential from plastic bag bans and urbanization.

articles.title: Township Tech: What Is Now Driving Financial Inclusion In South Africa's Informal Economy
articles.author: Forbes Africa
articles.content:
From the tin-roofed tenements to digital gold, these South African townships are embracing Bitcoin as a part of daily life, a FORBES AFRICA exclusive reveals. These emerging Bitcoin circular economies are delivering financial empowerment and literacy to communities long underserved or excluded from formal banking.
On the hillside, the tin roofs rattle in the sea breeze. Residents shuffle along the squalid streets as the children play with improvised toys. Beneath them, by the cliffs, the Indian Ocean is raw, untamed and roaring.
It’s a panoramic ocean view that people pay millions for a few kilometers west, perching their glass-walled homes facing the dramatic sea. But not here. The sea is free, and as far as the eyes can see.
It’s a week before Christmas in 2025, and we’re on South Africa’s south coast, in Isinyoka, a precinct within a township known locally as JCC Camp. The township, located in Mossel Bay—where coastal living meets the country’s famed Garden Route—is breezy and buzzing with activity.
The local hair salon wraps up its fourth booking for the day, and nearby, the spazas—informal supermarkets—see a steady stream of customers stepping in and out with aerated sodas and snacks in colorful packets. Animated chatter rents the air.
Loading...
It’s a similar scene playing out across Africa’s townships and informal settlements. The predictable hum of daily life, where the residents have limited means and cash is still king; where money is still saved in stokvels or under mattresses and investments are a foreign concept; where entire communities are still unbanked or underserved by the banking institutions; and where financial inclusion is still a far-fetched dream.
But in Isinyoka, things are slightly different.
Just before midday, the familiar crinkle of cash exchanging hands is nowhere to be heard. Instead, a catchy ring authorizes payments settled in seconds.
It’s the sound of Bitcoin.
With shop walls so thin, the digital pinging note joins the crash of the waves and the cries of the seagulls as the daily soundtrack of the township. It’s remarkable witnessing such an advanced payment ritual becoming second nature in a setting far removed from the urban world.
A Bitcoin circular economy has found its footing here, proselytizing and mainstreaming a community from the fringes to financial empowerment.
This has become possible thanks to the initiatives of Bitcoin Ekasi, an offshoot of The Surfers Kids, a non-profit (NPO) youth organization that provides free daily surfing and skateboarding lessons to children from the township.
Almost every day, around 40 kids make their way from Isinyoka to the NPO’s headquarters in Diaz Beach on the western side of Cape Point, where they are offered breakfast before surf lessons begin. And if the ocean doesn’t play ball, they skate the ‘Bitcoin Bowl’, their skating bowl funded by Jack Dorsey’s Block Discovery Grant (a philanthropic program run by the former Twitter CEO’s company Block). Some days, surfing follows the skating.
These activities bear no link to Bitcoin, but is imperative to Bitcoin Ekasi’s mission–and its story.
Hermann Vivier, the Founder and Chairman of Bitcoin Ekasi, shares with FORBES AFRICA how it all came to be. “A successful effort depends on what you start with,” he says, implying that a hub, be it a social enterprise, sports club, or a local hangout, is a foundation that’s literally a springboard to other things.
Starting small, in 2021, The Surfers Kids began paying its instructors—also residents of the neighboring township—in Bitcoin. The fundamental challenge was equipping Isinyoka’s shops and merchants with compatible payment systems, enabling the recipients to use Bitcoin as if it were hard cash.
Vivier reminisces that the pushback was instant. The apprehensions about Bitcoin were many. “Where does it go?” Nosihle Sakela, the owner of Kwallo’s shop, the first spaza store in JCC Camp to accept Bitcoin, tells FORBES AFRICA of her original reservations about the digital currency.
Tasked with educating the community about the new payment system, Luthando Ndabambi, Bitcoin Ekasi’s Project Community Lead, recalls it was very difficult explaining the premise of Bitcoin. “Everyone thought it was a scam,” says Ndabambi.
Financial autonomy must be an alien concept when life has been spent on the outside of a regulated monetary system.
“Most of the community don’t have bank accounts,” Nomsa Williams, who takes Bitcoin diploma classes under Bitcoin Ekasi’s umbrella, attests.
While the locals battled to internalize Bitcoin, Vivier remained patient, and persistent. Ironically, his fascination for the currency began after a Bitcoin crash plummeted his first investment by 80% in 2015. He gave himself an ultimatum: “Either I’ve just lost a lot of money, or I need to understand what it takes to make a more informed decision.”
His background in philosophy, which he studied at university, spurred his curiosity. “I like to understand what the problem is and not the symptoms. People point at symptoms when that is not the problem; it’s the symptom of the problem, which is a deeper thing,” Vivier explains in a cryptic manner.
It led him to dissect the 2008 global financial crisis. “The problem in the system became apparent to me then,” he recalls. “If you’re going to impose restrictions on financial access because of regulations that need to meet international standards, then you’re going to make it expensive to access the financial system, that’s just inevitable… You can’t have an accessible, cheap financial system [with] a mountain of red tape because that adds on extra costs.”
For Vivier, the penny dropped when unraveling Bitcoin’s permissionless layer, the result of a decentralized ledger running on an impenetrable blockchain.
For Isinyoka’s residents, it was about being able to relate. Simplifying Bitcoin proved tricky until, Vivier shares, Bitcoin Ekasi showed people how to buy airtime. “I would watch people in the township in the early days, and it was like a lightbulb went off. That direct, immediate impact!”
They programmed and created bitcoin bank accounts for around 50 children, who, once a week, spend the money at retailers already onboarded on to the new technology. “That would have been impossible to do with traditional banking systems,” Vivier explains.
Today, as many as 500 JCC Camp residents use Bitcoin regularly. Walk through the township, and Bitcoin art and graffiti leap from the exteriors of the tin-walled homes as loud political campaign posters.
Except that in this case, it’s a vote for financial sovereignty—and it’s working.
“It’s done a lot of good for my community,” Ndabambi, a resident of JCC Camp, affirms. “I see a lot of people who have started saving. Before Bitcoin, they didn’t care about saving because they didn’t trust the banks. It’s easy to save on Bitcoin because you have full control of your money. It has changed my life a lot!”
Mingling with Ndabambi’s peers, from the shopkeepers to the adolescents in the streets, it becomes clear that the overriding theme of what Bitcoin offers, as Silulami Dlayedwa, who manages Bitcoin Ekasi’s second-hand clothes store, puts it, is “financial freedom”.
“It allows you to think by yourself to better your future and not depend on anyone else,” elaborates Dlayedwa. “It feels like having your own power.”
Bongani Thebe, one of the first students to enrol in and pass Bitcoin Ekasi’s diploma course, offers another anecdote: “Bitcoin is for everyone!”
Like much of sub-Saharan Africa (SSA)—according to World Bank data, only 49% of people own a bank account—financial inclusion had eluded Thebe.
Unlike the myriad prerequisites of legacy banking institutions, Bitcoin’s low barriers to entry, requiring minimal personal information and a basic smart device, unlock a decentralized network where cross-border payments ensue at a fraction of the price (and time) than central banks.
In a region where intra-African remittances reach around $20 billion annually, with transfer costs among the highest in the world, that’s some consolation.
“You’re able to give people access to this system [Bitcoin] because it’s not burdened by regulation,” Vivier highlights.
Five years since integrating their first shop, Bitcoin Ekasi’s reach extends across JCC Camp, which includes Isinyoka, Isazane and Fairview, and into neighboring precincts. In the township, you can use Bitcoin at the car wash or repair shop, at the restaurant, the grocery, the pharmacy, as well as to settle school fees.
It’s now the norm and no longer a futuristic concept, creating a level playing field that democratizes money.
Bitcoin Ekasi’s financial crusade also transcends education. The Bitcoin Ekasi Center, nestled in between the tin roof-tenements, is the beating heart of this agenda.
Williams offers classes on Bitcoin alongside English and mathematics lessons. Additionally, she presents at local schools, spreading the word about digital money.
“The most important thing is to fill the gap of financial education because it’s not normally done here,” Williams says.
The Bitcoin Ekasi Center also doubles as a top-up hub, where locals can convert coins and notes into Satoshis (Sats)—the smallest denomination of Bitcoin—and load them on to their Bitcoin cards at the in-house, old-payphone-style ATM.
By blending access with education, the tiny township overlooking the Indian Ocean is in sync with a financial tool that, like the seas, offers myriad possibilities.
From Niche To Norm
Heading inland, around 1,200 kilometers north-east, yet another Bitcoin circular economy has risen amid penury. SowetoBTC, a non-profit initiative, is spearheading Bitcoin education here.
An offspring of Bitcoin Ekasi, it resides within the hustle and bustle of South Africa’s largest township, Soweto. Here too, on the outskirts of Johannesburg, widely dubbed the City of Gold, a shiny (figuratively) new tool is garnering traction.
“After visiting Bitcoin Ekasi, I got to see how other underprivileged communities have adopted a new form of money, money not controlled by the government,” Michael Rathebe, the founder of SowetoBTC, tells FORBES AFRICA. “It brought a new understanding as to how I can replicate the same within my own community in Soweto.”
In the Meadowlands precinct, where orange dust swirls past dilapidated homes, Rathebe took a page out of Vivier’s playbook, first founding a hub from which to expand from.
This led to Trezor Academy. The early days consisted of Bitcoin learning sessions, which still remain integral to operations. Today, it hosts over 100 residents, and ultimately, Rathebe reveals, “led to establishing the SowetoBTC learning center to empower Soweto’s youth with financial literacy through Bitcoin education programs”.
He admits his footprint is small, but having begun in 2024, is optimistic about the future. Adoption is growing.
“Many are starting to understand the challenges of financial exclusion and are embracing this new technology of Bitcoin as a life raft,” he adds.
At the time of writing, SowetoBTC had onboarded six small businesses, including spaza shops, fast food outlets, and a local company offering outdoor trash clearing services.
Like Bitcoin Ekasi, SowetoBTC offers Bitcoin diplomas to young people of ages from 10 and 35. “Those who participate are rewarded with Sats on a regular basis to spend at local Bitcoin-accepting businesses, or to save,” he notes.
A tangible ecosystem, SowetoBTC hasn’t just opened its doors to host financial seminars; it’s striving to shift the needle.
“Bitcoin has been a game-changer for Soweto’s youth,” Rathebe reports. “It’s provided them with the knowledge and skills required to change their mindset, from being just job-seekers to thinking as global participants, from been financially excluded to considering that since the financial system was not designed for them, they can relatively opt out and adopt another global financial system that’s open, permissionless and decentralized… The community is now able to control and decide its financial future without relying on a system designed to impoverish them.”
More Continental Momentum
Around 600 kilometers east, as the crow flies, another circular economy is gaining ground, also closing the divide when it comes to access to banking and financial services.
This time, it’s in Mozambique’s capital of Maputo, fringed by the Indian Ocean.
Here, Bitcoin Famba pulls the strings, organizing meet-ups, workshops, and bringing together Bitcoin-compliant businesses, from barbers to clothing stores, juice stands to factories, and grocery shops to tourism businesses.
Following a multifaceted formula like its peers, this Mozambican non-profit merges learning with play, doing so across three provinces: Maputo, Matutuíne, and Inhambane.
Embedded in some of the regions’ most disadvantaged communities, it regularly hosts skate sessions and surf lessons—harnessing activity to serve as a platform for teaching Bitcoin’s ethos.
“These environments include informal neighborhoods, youth communities, and small business clusters where access to reliable financial services is often limited and many transactions are still cash-based,” Daniel Taju, Founder of Bitcoin Famba, shares with FORBES AFRICA.
Most of their participants are students, informal workers, and entrepreneurs between 16 and 36 years old.
Mozambique’s social dilemma mirrors much of the continent. Its GDP leans on an informal economy that, for the most part, finds itself an outcast of the traditional banking system. In Maputo and beyond, Bitcoin offers a solution. “It’s creating new forms of economic access and opportunity,” Taju reveals. “For people who have been excluded from traditional financial systems, it allows them to receive payments, save value, and participate in the global digital economy using only a mobile phone.”
Simple by design, the digital currency has presented a financial gateway to communities previously locked out.
“We see Bitcoin in Africa evolving from a niche technology into critical financial infrastructure, especially in regions where traditional systems are expensive, slow, or inaccessible,” Taju says.
But to achieve Taju’s vision, perceptions must change.
‘Changed The Fundamental Rules’
Society’s relationship with Bitcoin has become something of a glorified get-rich scheme as investors hold on and hope for a 2013 repeat—the year of the bull (run).
Without Wall Street’s consent, Bitcoin birthed overnight millionaires; priced at $13.22 on January 1, it reached $1,132 on November 29 that year, an 8,547% rise that would convert a $10,000 investment into $854,700—it remains the most explosive rally in its history.
More infamous bull runs have followed, first in 2017 and then in 2020-2021, further cementing it as an investment haven rather than as a go-to transaction instrument.
Normalizing it as everyday currency, where users make daily payments, send remittances, and save, is arguably the biggest hurdle to achieving a legacy framework top-to-bottom.
“The future is not only about holding Bitcoin, but about using it in everyday economic activity,” Taju insists, surely aware of the complete psychological overhaul that this requires.
While regular, widespread usage would accelerate adoption efforts, Carel van Wyk, CEO and Co-founder of MoneyBadger, one of Africa’s leading Bitcoin payments companies, says to FORBES AFRICA: “The biggest blocker remains the number of people with Bitcoin to spend; most people will not spend an investment. But Bitcoin is more than that.”
Another prerequisite is connectivity, with some 600 million sub-Saharan Africans living without reliable access to power. Those unable to turn on the lights couldn’t even use Bitcoin if they tried.
As it captured global attention, Bitcoin’s rise sparked a cryptocurrency boom, but while the two resemble each other, Vivier believes it would be naive to view them as the same.
“Bitcoin and crypto are entirely different things,” he makes sure to point out. The stark difference is Bitcoin’s decentralized network, which makes it “almost impossible to change the rules”. Another is scarcity: only 21 million coins exist.
On the contrary, cryptocurrency is typically run by “software companies tightly controlled by directors, founders and investors”, Vivier notes. “Almost without exception, in the world of crypto, there are a few individuals who can essentially make a decision to change the rules at the click of a button.”
It’s a technocratic model more likened to a central bank than Bitcoin. Such authority was evident when Ethereum, a leading cryptocurrency, transitioned from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake in 2022, profoundly altering how the network validates transactions and secures itself.
“It changed the fundamental rules of the network instantly,” Vivier adds. The seismic shift wiped out Ethereum’s lucrative mining economy as large holders welcomed more influence from a boardroom move that challenged long-standing notions of blockchain security. Despite regulatory concerns, many cryptocurrencies share Bitcoin’s ideology of pursuing borderless rails that bypass governments’ costly, time-absorbing interventions. However, Bitcoin’s self-governing structure is unique.
“It’s human nature when you create something valuable, you tend to want to keep hold of it, which is why it’s so special that Satoshi Nakamoto made this world-changing technology [Bitcoin] and then walked away,” Vivier emphasizes, alluding to the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, Nakamoto, who published the whitepaper in 2008 and then mysteriously vanished.
When it comes to solving Africa’s banking crisis, Bitcoin circular economies are a start, but it’s not the endgame (and it’s not without its cynics).
In essence, a circular economy typically thrives in a contained environment. Vivier puts it more bluntly: “Circular economies are not meant to scale to huge numbers, they are a proof of concept.”
Bitcoin Ekasi is an African case study worth noting, one that suggests Bitcoin to be tailor-made for the region, offering grassroots avenues central banks can’t reach.
Clearly, a domino effect is in motion—the road to adoption is being paved as we speak. According to Chainanalysis data, SSA is the third-fastest-growing crypto region worldwide, recording over $205 billion in on-chain value between July 2024 and June 2025, marking a 52% increase from the previous year. Within this growth, Bitcoin emerged as the number one stream, accounting for 89% and 74% of Nigeria’s and South Africa’s crypto purchases, the continent’s largest digital money markets by total value received, exceeding $90 billion and $35 billion, respectively.
Africa’s Accelerating Bitcoin Rally
Meanwhile, innovation is scaling the ways we use electronic cash. The Bitcoin Lightning Network enables near-instant, low-cost, cross-border payments, mimicking informal markets’ desire for cash-in-hand business, meaning, if a trader from Accra visits a fabric store in Lagos, they can deal in real-time.
“Lightning settles payments in less than a second,” Theophilus Isah, Co-founder of Mavapay, a Lagos-based Bitcoin lightning payment platform, echoes to FORBES AFRICA.
Explaining its speedy mechanics, Isah depicts the more immediate journey of a lightning payment: “It doesn’t follow the methodology of bitcoin payments. What do I mean by that? With Bitcoin payments, you have addresses and transactions. With lightning, you really only have payments because you are paying for an invoice. You request payment; somebody fulfils that invoice.”
As technology advances, Africa’s Bitcoin rally is accelerating at an all-encompassing pace. Formal markets are seemingly warming to Bitcoin as a trusted tool.
In South Africa, a partnership reportedly signed last October, between payments provider Scan to Pay and MoneyBadger, onboarded 650,000 outlets, including major retail chains, Vodacom, Makro, and Shoprite.
A touch ahead of the curb was Pick n Pay, a leading South African supermarket chain that, in 2023, made over 1,500 stores Bitcoin-compatible.
Whether goods and services will be priced in Bitcoin as a unit of account in the future, Van Wyk believes will “require a level of economic and cultural change that will take considerable time”.
While leading retailers establish gateways, institutional integration is taking shape. Such heavyweight endorsement opens a new realm of capital and interest, ushering in regulatory frameworks that enable businesses and individuals to invest and spend with confidence.
In an ecosystem prone to price shocks, stability is the currency investors trust.
The Africa Bitcoin Corporation (ABC), the continent’s first listed Bitcoin treasury company, formed in 2025, is leading the region’s upper echelon adoption.
So much so that it played a pivotal role in remodeling outdated regulations, including Investable Weight Factors (IWF) on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE). “Prior to this work, there was no clear regulatory pathway for a JSE-listed entity to hold Bitcoin on its balance sheet in a manner that was compliant, disclosed, and investable,” Warren Wheatley, ABC’s CEO, discloses to FORBES AFRICA.
“It brings Bitcoin into the formal savings and investment ecosystem for the first time,” he adds, alluding to the fact that South African institutions or high-net-worth investors no longer need to head offshore to hold Bitcoin.
That’s not to say regulation is perfect. African corporations face an uphill battle with governments that have yet to fully grasp digital currencies, fostering fragmented environments with outmoded policies.
So, while South Africa has some of the world’s most progressive jurisdictions for digital money, there’s a need to create a uniform framework for Africa, one that could be introduced through the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement as the continent moves to becoming the world’s largest single market.
Achieving widespread adoption isn’t a certainty, but there’s a trajectory that suggests it’s no longer out of the question.
Housing large crypto platforms, including Yellow Card and Luno, Africa’s ecosystem has entered legitimization—safe, efficient and reputable—establishing a level of credibility that can no longer be ignored.
On the ground, there’s more work to do.
Scores of domestic banks remain skeptical about accepting digital currencies, insinuating their bubble of protection over the fiat system is still seriously intact. Pop the barrier, and hyperscaling surely spurts. That being said, several leading African banks are embracing cryptocurrencies, most notably entities such as Absa Group.
Pessimists will be the first to point out Bitcoin’s price volatility as a dissuasion to it becoming a primary payment medium. It is erratic in value, but does that not indicate a world increasingly intrigued?
“Bitcoin has always been subject to extreme price swings and will continue to be volatile while it is still priced in government fiat currencies,” Van Wyk explains, before mentioning that “volatility is not purely a Bitcoin problem, and I expect hedge funds will continue to capitalize on it for a long time to come”.
“Compared with failing fiat systems, capital restrictions, and chronic currency debasement, Bitcoin can still be the better tool,” he adds.
Market crashes haven’t deterred the masses because there’s a resounding feeling of something bigger than Bitcoin; the beginnings of an entire monetary system trotting towards decentralization, where a young man from rural Malawi, previously limited by central banks’ identification protocols, has permissionless access at his fingertips.
When it comes to altering something as historic as money, Bitcoin’s 17-year existence pales in comparison to a centuries-old financial system ingrained in society. The human psyche often urges us to avoid change, favoring the security of stability.
But when many Africans have never felt financial upliftment, change isn’t just needed, it’s in the continent’s best interest. It’s a region where traditional banking is exclusive, but its burgeoning population is tech-conscious; an environment where millions are online, but unbanked.
Bitcoin has proven it can bridge this gap.
Walk amongst the tin houses of JCC Camp, and you’ll notice its growing influence. In a place of segregation, it has unlocked independence.
The air might be salty, but the future here is fresh and liberating.
A one-size-fits-all solution rarely works in Africa’s favor. Bitcoin might just be the one that does.

Clarios has completed the acquisition of three battery recycling centers from Ecobat in Germany and Austria, expanding its recycling footprint in Europe and strengthening its closed-loop battery supply chain.
With all regulatory approvals finalized, Clarios is integrating recycling operations in Freiberg and Braubach in Germany and Arnoldstein in Austria, reinforcing its role in the circular economy and supporting Europe’s ambition for more sustainable and resilient industrial value chains.
Expanded Recycling Capacity and Materials Recovery
The additional facilities increase Clarios’ ability to recover critical materials, including lead and polypropylene, and reuse them in the production of new low-voltage batteries. This strengthens supply security while reducing reliance on primary raw materials and lowering the environmental footprint across the battery lifecycle.
“This acquisition is a strategic step forward for Clarios in Europe,” said Werner Benade, president of Clarios EMEA. “By expanding our recycling and material recovery capabilities, we are building a more resilient and sustainable supply chain that supports upcoming EU battery regulations and delivers real environmental benefits for customers and communities alike.”
Supporting EU Circular Economy and Vehicle and Battery Regulations
Clarios said the integration brings several strategic advantages:
- Expanded Lead Recycling Capacity: Enabling closed loop recovery of materials from end of life batteries at greater scale.
- Polypropylene Recycling and Compounding: Establishing Clarios’ first in house polypropylene compounding capability, aligned with EU requirements for recycled plastic content in automotive applications.
- Stronger European Supply Chain Resilience: Enhancing regional recycling and material processing capabilities to meet growing demand for sustainable battery solutions.
With the expanded recycling network, Clarios said it’s advancing its commitment to a fully integrated, closed-loop business model—helping ensure that millions of vehicles across Europe are powered by batteries made with responsibly sourced and recycled materials.

articles.title: Marwynn Holdings Announces Strategic Expansion into Battery Recycling Infrastructure with Plans for EcoLoopX Black Mass Production Facility - Batteries News
articles.author: Batteries News
articles.content:
Marwynn Holdings Announces Strategic Expansion into Battery Recycling Infrastructure with Plans for EcoLoopX Black Mass Production Facility
IRVINE, CA / ACCESS Newswire / May 1, 2026 / Marwynn Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq:MWYN) today announced a major evolution of its EcoLoopX platform with plans to develop its first physical processing facility dedicated to the production of “Black Mass” – a critical intermediate material in the lithium-ion battery recycling value chain.
The planned facility marks a strategic transition for EcoLoopX Corporation, a subsidiary of MWYN, from an asset-light logistics platform to an operational participant in the battery materials sector. By processing end-of-life (EoL) batteries and manufacturing scrap into black mass, MWYN expects to recover and concentrate high-value minerals including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese.
Strengthening the Circular Economy
The global surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption and portable electronics has created a massive supply-chain bottleneck for battery-grade minerals. EcoLoopX’s move into black mass production is designed to help address this challenge as one part of a broader industry effort by:
- Capturing Higher Value: Moving upstream from simple e-waste collection to the high-margin production of battery-ready feedstock.
- Proprietary Mechanical Processing: Utilizing shredding and separation technology to produce high-purity black mass for downstream hydrometallurgical refiners.
- Closed-Loop Integration: Feeding the recovered materials back into the technology supply chain, potentially supporting the hardware requirements of MWYN’s AI-focused subsidiary, NexaCore Technologies.
Leadership Commentary
Yin Yan, CEO of Marwynn Holdings, said,
This is the natural next step for our circular economy strategy,
“While logistics and trading gave us the foothold, building our own processing capacity allows us to capture a significantly larger portion of the battery lifecycle value. Our black mass facility will serve as a bridge between the waste of today and the high-tech batteries of tomorrow.”
Operational Roadmap
MWYN is currently evaluating several strategic locations for the facility, prioritizing regions with high densities of electronic scrap and favorable regulatory environments for green-tech manufacturing. The company expects to finalize site selection and initiate the permitting process by the third quarter of 2026.

articles.content:
Mike Biddle, Evok Innovations
Dr. Mike Biddle is the Managing Director of Evok Innovations, an entrepreneur-led cleantech venture fund that aims to increase the scale, diversity, and quality of early-stage innovations focused on renewable energy, reducing the time it takes to commercialize technologies. Evok accomplishes this by connecting entrepreneurs with flexible capital, mentors, and industry partners. Before Evok, Mike founded MBA Polymers—literally from his garage. He grew MBA Polymers to the world’s leading multinational company recovering plastics from end-of-life durable goods, such as computers, electronics, appliances, automobiles, and now household waste.
Mike received a B.S. in chemical engineering from the University of Louisville and a Ph.D. in polymer science and engineering from Case Western Reserve University, both with high honors. He was also a Sloan Fellow at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business, graduating with an M.S. in management science. Mike has won numerous international awards, including the 2017 SME Circulars Award and the Davos Prize at the World Economic Forum.
Matt Terwillegar, Danimer Scientific
Matt Terwillegar has been in product development for 25 years, specifically in the field of biotechnology for ten years. He specializes in application development of bioplastics, biocomposites, and bio-based coatings. He began his career as a product development chemist at Reichhold in 1996, worked as a plant engineer at Piedmont Chemical in High Point, North Carolina, and then as an application development manager at Myriant Corporation. He has recently joined Danimer Scientific as product engineer.
Matt holds a B.S. in organic chemistry from Rollins College in Winter Park, FL and an M.S. in chemical engineering from the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.
Bill Orts, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Services
Dr. William J. Orts is the Research Leader for Bioproducts at the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Services Western Regional Research Center where he oversees a team that aims to add optimal value to agricultural coproducts, especially from under-valued biomass sources found in the Western United States. He has over 30 years of experience in research related to biofuels and bioproducts with over 200 publications and more than 125 invited presentations.
Bill's masters work focused on fermentation scale-up of gums derived from wood sugars and Ph.D. research carried out at the Xerox Research labs on developing polyhydroxyalkanoates as a commercial biopolymer.
Amy Waun, Procter & Gamble
Amy Waun is a Senior Scientist in the Corporate R&D Division of The Procter & Gamble Company (P&G) in Cincinnati, Ohio. She earned her Ph.D. in materials engineering and science from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech) and her B.S. in chemistry from the University of Notre Dame. Amy is a member of the P&G team staffed full-time to support PureCycle Technologies. She applies her academic training and more than 17 years of industrial experience in chemistry and materials science and engineering to lead the polymer analytical characterization for feedstock selection, process development, and product development for PureCycle Technologies.
Frédérique Guillamot, Carbios
Frédérique Guillamot holds a Ph.D. in environmental biosciences from Marseille University (France) and joined Carbios in 2012. As Innovation Manager, she is responsible for identifying and implementing innovative projects. Carbios, a French cleantech company listed on the Paris stock exchange, has successfully completed a five-year, multi-million euro collaborative R&D program and is now moving to industrialization with two disruptive biological innovations that provide solutions for the end-of-life of polymers. In particular, Frédérique is involved in the management of Carbios’ process of infinitely recycling polyester (PET) without any quality loss.
Gregg T. Beckham, National Renewable Energy Laboratory
Gregg T. Beckham is a Senior Research Fellow and Group Leader at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. He received his Ph.D. in chemical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2007. Gregg currently leads and works with an interdisciplinary team of biologists, chemists, and engineers at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory on green processes and products using chemistry and biology, including in the areas of biomass conversion and plastics upcycling.
Stacy Katz, Waste Management
Stacy Katz is Waste Management’s Senior Manager of Materials Management and Quality. In this role, Stacy leads the quality program for Waste Management’s recycling business. Stacy is responsible for improving the quality of material received at Waste Management recycling facilities from customers, as well as the quality of sorted commodities produced. She develops and implements strategic planning initiatives and identifies operational improvements that increase the quality and quantity of material diverted from the waste stream. Prior to this position, Stacy was Waste Management’s Municipal Manager of Recycling and Diversion for the Western Group, where her focus was to increase the volume of recyclables from municipalities throughout the West and she was previously a Senior Environmental Consultant focusing on zero waste initiatives with large corporate clients.
Stacy holds a master’s degree in environmental science and management and has experience in zero waste initiatives, program and product management and has designed and implemented both environmental and business solutions.
Jason Locklin, University of Georgia
Jason Locklin obtained his B.S. from Millsaps College in 1999. He graduated with his M.S. in chemistry from University of Alabama at Birmingham in 2002 and Ph.D. from the University of Houston in 2004. Jason then went on as a Director of Central Intelligence Postdoctoral Scholar at Stanford University in 2005 in the Department of Chemical Engineering. In 2007, Locklin joined the University of Georgia in the Department of Chemistry and the College of Engineering and was promoted to Professor in 2018. He founded the New Materials Institute in 2016 that focuses on green engineering principles and circular materials management.
Jason has been awarded the Central Intelligence Agency Young Investigator Award (2007), National Science Foundation CAREER Award (2010), the Northeast Georgia American Chemical Society Chemist of the Year for Research (2009–2010), and the Atlanta Magazine Groundbreaker Award (2011). He is a Distinguished Faculty Scholar in the College of Engineering and the Site Director for the National Science Foundation Industry University Collaborative Research Center—Center for Bioplastics and Biocomposites at the University of Georgia.
Scott Farling, Titus MRF Services
Scott Farling is the Vice President of Business Development and Research for Titus MRF Services, a leading systems integrator for the waste and recycling industry and developer of secondary material recovery facilities. After more than a decade working in the specialty chemicals industry, Scott shifted careers to follow his passion and focus on recycling and recovering value from complex waste streams with MBA Polymers, Inc. and Agilyx Corporation. In addition to his work with Titus, he co-founded the Ocean Plastics Recovery Project and is working to clean up the oceans and coastlines and find end-of-life recycling and recovery solutions for ocean plastics.
Scott holds a B.S. in chemical engineering with a minor in environmental engineering from The Pennsylvania State University.
Eric Klingenberg, Mars Advanced Research Institute
Eric has a B.S in chemistry with a minor in biology from Geneva College and a Ph.D. in polymer chemistry from The Pennsylvania State University. During his 20+ year career as an industrial researcher and R&D leader, he has worked in multiple fields of study, including new material development, manufacturing scale-up, and process optimization.
Currently, Eric is part of the Mars Advanced Research Institute (MARI) where he leads the Materials Science Platform. His interests include the development of new materials and processes to reduce the environmental impact of plastic packaging. He also serves on several university advisory boards and is a technical advisor for the Center for Hierarchical Materials Design, a consortium of national labs and universities working to develop and expand the use of data and computation tools to accelerate advanced materials design.
Cristina Negri, Argonne National Laboratory
Cristina Negri is the Director of the Environmental Science Division at Argonne National Laboratory where she leads its strategic programmatic direction inclusive of a diverse research portfolio in environmental sciences. As a scientist, her current work focuses on developing innovative land-use approaches and functional landscapes to achieve environmental services, conservation, and input-efficient bioenergy crop feedstocks, and to leverage productive use impaired/marginal land and polluted water resources both in urban and agricultural contexts. Her interests lie in finding solutions that embrace reuse and recycling and apply them to find practical solutions to address global growth under limited resources.
Jill Martin, Dow Chemical Company
Jill Martin is a global sustainability fellow at the Dow Chemical Company. For the past 25 years, she has served in both research and development and technical service and development in the performance plastics field. Jill is a member of the Michigan State University and California Polytechnic State University Packaging Advisory Boards and serves on the ISTA Global Advisory Board.
Jill received her bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering from Carnegie Mellon University and a Ph.D. in polymer engineering and science from Case Western Reserve University, where her research focused on structure/property relationships in polyethylenes, a field she has continued to work in during her career with Dow.

Market Size and Transformation Trajectory:
The projected expansion from USD 15.5 billion in 2026 to nearly USD 40 billion by 2036 signals more than growth it reflects a structural transformation in packaging materials.
Bioplastics are transitioning from:
• Premium alternatives → to compliance-driven necessities
• Niche applications → to high-volume packaging formats
This shift is particularly evident in bottles, films, and flexible packaging, where brands can visibly demonstrate sustainability commitments.
Key Growth Drivers
1. Regulatory Pressure Is Now a Market Catalyst
Global bans and restrictions on single-use plastics are no longer theoretical-they are operational constraints.
Governments across Europe and Asia are mandating:
• Compostable or recyclable packaging
• Reduced plastic intensity
• Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) compliance
This is forcing packaging redesign at scale.
2. Corporate Net-Zero Commitments
Large FMCG and beverage companies are embedding carbon reduction targets into procurement decisions. Bioplastics-especially drop-in solutions like Bio PET-offer:
• Lower lifecycle emissions
• Compatibility with existing recycling systems
• Immediate integration without retooling
3. Consumer-Driven Sustainability Economics
Sustainability is no longer just a branding lever-it influences purchase decisions and brand loyalty.
Packaging is increasingly viewed as:
• A visible sustainability signal
• A differentiator in competitive categories like beverages and personal care
Market Reality Check: Constraints That Still Matter
Despite strong growth, the market faces structural challenges:
Cost Premiums
Bioplastics remain more expensive than conventional plastics due to:
• Feedstock limitations (biomass supply)
• Smaller production scale
• Complex processing requirements
Feedstock Competition
Agricultural inputs used for bioplastics (e.g., corn, sugarcane) compete with:
• Food supply chains
• Biofuel production
This creates volatility in pricing and supply.
Infrastructure Gaps
Not all bioplastics are equally scalable. Materials must align with:
• Existing recycling systems
• Industrial composting infrastructure
Without this alignment, adoption slows.

By Material

The dominant segment due to:
• Drop-in compatibility
• Recycling infrastructure alignment
• Proven performance in bottles
• PLA & PHA
Emerging as next-generation biodegradable solutions, especially for:
• Flexible packaging
• Compostable applications
By Application

The leading segment because:
• Beverage packaging offers high-volume adoption
• Infrastructure is already optimized for PET formats
• Brands use bottles as visible sustainability milestones
By End Use
• Food & Beverages (52.7%)
The largest consumer of bioplastics, driven by:
• Shelf-life requirements
• Regulatory scrutiny
• Consumer visibility
Regional Analysis: Where Growth Is Accelerating
Asia-Pacific: The Growth Engine
• India (10.9% CAGR) and China (10.5%) lead global expansion

• Government plastic bans
• Rapid urbanization
• Expanding packaging consumption

• Strongest policy-driven adoption

• Circular economy mandates
• Plastic reduction targets
North America: Corporate-Led Transition
• Growth driven by:
• Sustainability commitments from major brands
• Innovation in advanced materials
• Increasing investment in domestic biomanufacturing

articles.title: Achieving Circularity: Turning Waste Into Solid Profit
articles.author: Supply Chain Brain
articles.content:
Analyst Insight: The days are over when firms could view cutting waste or recycling output as just reputational proof of green ambition. Regulators are forcing circular economy models up CEOs’ agendas; but, just as important, companies must see this as a strategic lever to bolster margins.
Circularity — reducing, reusing or recycling waste — is at the heart of business conversations in 2026 that are focused on cost control, supply chain resilience and protecting margins. These are existential issues for companies everywhere in a fast-changing and volatile world economy.
There’s been a visible shift in executive attention. The Conference Board’s recent survey of CEO and C-suite ESG priorities shows resource efficiency, circularity and clean technology investment all ranking ahead of greenhouse gas reduction. That’s not a signal of declining concern for the climate. Rather, it reflects a stronger focus on actions that can more directly improve competitiveness, tighten operational discipline and reduce exposure to volatility.
For sure, closer regulatory scrutiny has played its part in grabbing business leaders’ attention to the issue. For example, in Europe, new rules under the EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation will, from July, 2026, bar large companies from destroying unsold clothes, shoes and fashion accessories. Smaller firms will be hit by the ban in 2030. A name-and-shame strategy will also oblige firms to disclose how much unsold stock they throw away.
Yet the external policy pressure should not obscure a straightforward internal commercial reality. Each year, an estimated 4% to 9% of clothes in Europe are destroyed before ever being worn. That’s not just a social issue, but a financial one: capital tied up in products that never generate revenue, alongside the embedded costs of materials, labor, transport and storage.
For many brands and retailers, stock destruction has acted as a safety valve, allowing them to manage forecasting errors, protect brand positioning and clear inventory. Better to burn last season’s designer dress than undercut the label’s margin by selling it cheap, or paying to store it till next year. Curbing that option changes the economics of overproduction. Excess stock becomes more visible, more expensive and more strategically relevant.
There will be short-term pressures. Companies may face higher warehousing and logistics costs, investments in inventory tracking and reporting systems, and expanded processes for redistribution or resale. Businesses with structurally high overproduction could experience margin compression as they adjust.
But focusing only on transition costs risks missing the broader opportunity: Waste is evidence of avoidable cost and operational inefficiency. Better demand forecasting reduces markdowns and write-offs. Shorter production runs and more flexible supply chains reduce working capital exposure. Resale, repair and refurbishment channels can recover value from goods that would previously have been written off.
Transparency adds another dimension. Once disclosure of unsold goods becomes standardized, inventory management outcomes become visible to investors, customers and other stakeholders. Disposal volumes shift from being an internal metric to a performance indicator. That visibility can influence investor confidence, procurement decisions and brand credibility.
The strategic question for leadership teams is therefore not simply how to comply, but how to compete under these new conditions.
Circularity initiatives that sit at the periphery of the business — disconnected from finance, supply chain and product design — are unlikely to deliver value. Those that are embedded into core decision-making stand a better chance of improving resilience and capital efficiency.
There are five practical actions that leadership teams can implement to strengthen their circularity strategy:
Quantify exposure. Establish a clear baseline of unsold inventory, return rates and disposal costs, including warehousing, handling and reputational risk.
Strengthen forecasting discipline. Invest in demand sensing, smaller production runs and faster replenishment cycles to reduce overproduction at source.
Create value-recovery pathways. Formalize processes for resale, repair, refurbishment and recycling so that excess stock becomes an asset to manage rather than a liability to eliminate.
Upgrade data and controls. Ensure inventory tracking and reporting systems are robust, auditable and aligned with finance and compliance requirements.
Integrate design and strategy. Product durability, repairability and material choices directly influence downstream costs and revenue recovery potential.
For global companies, alignment is critical. Operating dual systems for different markets is costly. Better to get the jump on an enterprise-wide circularity agenda than be pushed into it piecemeal, country by country. Regulatory developments in one major jurisdiction can quickly set the de facto global standard for inventory management, reporting and product design.
Circularity is no cure-all. It’s not a substitute for a broader environmental strategy to reduce emissions and pollutants. But the direction of travel is clear. Resource efficiency is moving from an add-on to the reputational narrative to being a must-have operational tool.
For companies navigating inflationary pressure, regulatory scrutiny and brand risk all at the same time, treating waste as a measurable and manageable business variable can be one of the most practical available levers of competitiveness.

articles.title: Turning pollution into products: Nzambi Matee’s circular economy innovation
articles.author: Daily Nation
articles.content:
What you need to know:
- Despite global recognition, Kenya’s circular economy innovators struggle to secure capital needed to scale and achieve profitability sustainably.
- Nzambi Matee’s journey highlights funding gaps, gender disparities and systemic barriers facing women entrepreneurs in manufacturing innovation sector.
When Nzambi Matee walked away from her job at Kenya’s National Oil Corporation in 2016, her family thought she had lost her mind. “Tell me, if people don’t quit their jobs in oil and gas to start dealing with plastic waste, that is the true blueprint of someone going mad,” she says, laughing at the memory.
Nzambi had been working in upstream oil data analysis, applying the physics she had studied at university. It was a secure, well‑paying job in one of the most lucrative industries in the world. But something was missing.
“My heart wasn’t in it. The passion, the desire; it was missing. I felt like something was lacking,” she says, punching her right hand into her left to emphasise just how deeply she longed to do what she truly wanted.
What she wanted was not merely to get by – doing an office job just to survive – but to leave a mark, a legacy characterised by strong conviction, much like the late Nobel laureate
In simple terms, a circular economy is about turning waste into value and keeping materials in use for as long as possible, instead of discarding them.
“My uncles and aunties told my mom, ‘Your child has gone loose.’ Even my mother asked me, ‘Are you sure you’re okay?’ But I told her, there is a method to the madness. You might not understand it now, but in time you will see.”
While some studies indicate that women make up roughly 60 per cent of Kenya’s informal waste workforce, many earning less than $2, concrete data on women engineers and innovators in the circular economy remains scarce.
Take Nzambi Matee. A materials engineer with a degree in Physics (Pure and Applied) from the Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology. Existing data largely captures women as informal recyclers, not as scientists, engineers, and entrepreneurs driving innovation in the sector.
The love for Physics
Born and raised in Nairobi, Nzambi represents the minds behind products made from recycled waste, solutions that transform materials that would otherwise harm communities.‘just do your physics homework,’ because biology was hopeless for me.”
When she joinedGlobal Gender Gap Report 2024 shows that in Kenya, women accounted for just 19.46 per cent of graduates in engineering, manufacturing, and construction.
For Nzambi, however, her love for physics made the path clear: She knew that was where she belonged.
While her family thought she needed a psychiatric assessment at a mental facility such as Mathare Hospital, Nzambi was deep in geophysical calculations, pushing her mind to its limits.
Her mother’s backyard became her laboratory. There, she took her first steps, building machines from scrap metal, before progressing to producing one or two paver blocks each day. She then moved to the next phase: walking from one construction site to another, seeking feedback from contractors and site engineers on her early prototype).
Even when some dismissed her, treating her efforts as a joke, she did not give up. She understood rejection was part of the process and refused to let it stand in her way. For the next nine months, she kept returning to construction sites, asking engineers to test her paver blocks.
The nine months
The kinder ones had something to tell her.‘No, change this, do this, do that.’ Every day I would take plastic, process it, make one or two paver blocks, and go to construction sites,” she says.
But scaling up required machinery, which required money. She drafted a business plan, secured letters of interest from contractors, and approached banks. Every single one said no.
“Banks are not in the business of funding innovation,” she reflects. “They are in the business of selling money.”
At her lowest point in 2017, she applied to the Watson Institute, an incubation programme focused on social entrepreneurship. To her surprise, she was accepted and spent a year there, from January to December 2018. At Watson, in collaboration with the University of Colorado, she gained access to advanced labs and mentors.
She refined her paver block design, built prototypes of new machinery, and secured seed capital from the institute.
She hired a team of four and built machines capable of producing hundreds a day. “I moved from producing 10 to producing 500 in a day. I was so happy. It was so nice,” she says.
Covid-19 and turning point
Then Covid-19 struck. She had just launched her product in March 2020 when Kenya went into lockdown.
With people stuck at home, demand for renovations surged. Gjenge pivoted to online sales and began supplying paver blocks for home projects.
The struggle for capital
Despite progress, breaking even has been a long, grinding struggle. Expansion requires patient capital [long‑term, low‑interest financing], but Kenya’s financial system is not designed to support manufacturing innovation, she says.
“We need cheap patient capital,” she insists. “That’s what boosted China’s manufacturing industry. Here, if you get a loan, by the time you’ve set up the machine and tested it, they’re already asking for repayment.”
Government institutions have also failed to step in, she says. “If there’s anyone who has the muscle to take us from this level to being bankable, it’s the government. But if they’re not going in this space, then who is?” she asks.
Impact investors, meanwhile, shy away from capital expenditure, she says. “They say we don’t invest in machinery. But without machinery, I can’t scale. It’s a Catch‑22.”
Her testimony reflects the funding realities faced by women innovators. A 2024 Kenya Innovation Outlook by the Kenya National Innovation Agency, a state corporation, highlights this challenge, showing that women-led startups secured only 12 per cent of total funding between 2019 and 2023.
While the report advocates for more inclusive innovation systems, Nzambi’s experience suggests that government agencies are still falling short in supporting women innovators.
Building machines from scratch
Part of her company’s uniqueness lies in its machines, which Nzambi designed herself with the help of engineers and a mentor. “I see machines in my head,” she says. “I run simulations in my mind. I draw sketches, even though I’m not good at drawing. Then we build prototypes, test them, iterate, break them down, and rebuild.”
Her machines are designed to handle the abrasive mix of plastic and sand, a process similar to extrusion but modified for construction materials.
Undeterred determination
From 2020 to 2023, she focused on proof of concept, testing her product in the market, refining processes, and building customer trust. “In manufacturing, you don’t just wake up and start growing. There are stages: prototyping, proof of concept, and then commercialisation.”
The company is now ready for commercialisation: mass production at scale. But that, she says, requires hundreds of millions in investment. Without it, operations remain small-scale, limiting their ability to meet growing demand.
Currently, she employs 30 full-time workers and about 250 others on temporary contracts, especially during projects involving the installation of paver blocks. With the right machinery, capable of producing more than 500 units in a single shift, the company could meet demand more efficiently and create more jobs.
At present, production runs 24 hours a day in three shifts. “The demand is not the problem,” she says. “The problem is supply. If we had the capital to scale, we could create jobs, reduce waste, and build affordable housing materials. But without it, we crawl.”
After nearly a decade of persistence, Nzambi has distilled her frustrations into three demands. “We need cheap, patient capital,” she says. “Loans with long moratoriums and low interest rates, the kind that gives manufacturing room to breathe.”
Her second task is to make serious investment in research and development (R&D) grants. She says, “R&D is the seed that shifts us from being a consumer market to a productive one. But here, no one finances R&D. To financiers, it looks like a waste of money. They don’t understand that it’s the genesis of everything.”
Finally, she calls on government institutions to rethink how they invest in innovative ventures, noting that “the state needs to support local machinery and innovation that doesn’t fit neatly into existing categories”.
Despite the obstacles, she remains undeterred. Still, she continues at her own pace, expanding slowly with the resources she can muster. “I will expand at my own pace using my own resources,” she says. “It will take more time than if provided with credit, but we will get there.”
articles.summary: What you need to know: - Despite global recognition, Kenya’s circular economy innovators struggle to secure capital needed to scale and achieve profitability sustainably. - Nzambi Matee’s journey highlights funding gaps, gender disparities and systemic barriers facing women entrepreneurs in manufacturing innovation sector. When Nzambi Matee walked away from her job at Kenya’s National Oil Corporation in 2016, her family thought she had lost her mind.

articles.title: Common EPR portal to anchor India’s recycling push as industry, NITI Aayog call for stronger implementation framework
articles.author: Down To Earth
articles.content:
The Union environment ministry is set to roll out a common Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal, a move aimed at streamlining compliance, improving traceability and scaling India’s recycling ecosystem, even as industry and policymakers flagged persistent gaps in implementation and institutional coordination.
The upcoming unified portal, under development by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), is expected to integrate multiple waste streams and address operational bottlenecks identified through extensive stakeholder consultations, an official said, at a conference on May 4, 2026. The platform is being designed to be more user-friendly and responsive to challenges faced by producers, recyclers and regulators.
The announcement comes as India deepens its reliance on EPR as a central policy tool to transition from a linear to a circular economy. According to Bharat Sharma, member secretary at Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the EPR framework now spans plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres, with digital certification systems improving transparency and tracking of recycling outcomes. Under the E-Waste Management Rules, 2022, the regime has shifted from a collection-based approach to a recycling-based system, covering over 100 categories of electronic equipment.
The proposed common portal is also expected to significantly expand participation, with estimates suggesting it could onboard up to 50 lakh (5 million) users across the solid waste management ecosystem, marking a major step in digitising compliance and market mechanisms.
Shobhit Srivastava, programme manager (industrial pollution), Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), says the CPCB’s move toward a common portal for seven sectors is a positive step to resolve industry concerns. The incorporation of GST and EPR integration is a welcome move that aligns with CSE’s recommendations.
“However, the portal’s success hinges on transparency. It must provide public access so that researchers and think tanks can independently assess progress and identify implementation challenges,” he adds.
While welcoming policy progress, the Material Recycling Association of India (MRAI) called for a dedicated national framework or nodal authority to address structural inefficiencies in the sector.
“India has developed some of the most forward-looking policies in the recycling space… however, the real challenge lies in ensuring consistent and effective implementation on the ground,” said Sanjay Mehta, president of MRAI.
He pointed to issues such as frequent administrative transfers, fragmented governance across ministries and inconsistent regulatory interpretation as key barriers to effective execution. The industry body argued that a centralised institutional mechanism could improve coordination, accelerate decision-making and ensure continuity in policy implementation.
MRAI also cautioned against a uniform approach to EPR across materials, noting that high-value recycling segmentssuch as non-ferrous metals may require more tailored regulatory frameworks to avoid disrupting efficient market-driven systems.
Echoing the need for stronger systems, Priyavrat Bhati, programme head at NITI Aayog, described the circular economy as a “strategic lever” for resource efficiency and industrial competitiveness, stressing the importance of institutionalising the sector.
He highlighted the need for stable demand for recycled materials, better enforcement and stronger integration of the informal sector — a recurring challenge across waste streams. NITI Aayog has been working on sector-specific strategies, including end-of-life vehicles, waste tyres and e-waste, to improve coordination and implementation.
Stakeholders broadly agreed that while India’s policy architecture on recycling is robust, the next phase must focus on execution, enforcement and ecosystem development.
Officials emphasised that beyond compliance, the sector must move towards efficient and value-driven recycling, including recovery of critical materials and deeper integration of informal waste collectors into formal systems.
Challenges remain in verification systems, infrastructure expansion and ensuring consistent regulatory signals. However, the proposed common EPR portal is seen as a key step towards addressing fragmentation and improving accountability across the recycling value chain.
articles.summary: The Union environment ministry is set to roll out a common Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal, a move aimed at streamlining compliance, improving traceability and scaling India’s recycling ecosystem, even as industry and policymakers flagged persistent gaps in implementation and institutional coordination.
