articles.title: Industry body seeks nodal authority for recycling, flags policy gaps
articles.author: Business Standard
articles.content:
Industry body seeks nodal authority for recycling, flags policy gaps
MRAI highlights fragmented oversight and execution challenges in recycling policies, urging a central nodal body to ensure continuity, coordination, and effective implementation
Listen to This Article
The Material Recycling Association of India (MRAI) has called for the creation of a centralised nodal authority or a dedicated ministry for recycling and circular economy, citing structural bottlenecks that are hindering effective policy implementation.
Drawing from industry experience, MRAI President Sanjay Mehta said frequent administrative transfers across ministries disrupt policy continuity, leading to inconsistent interpretation of regulations, delays in execution, and a disconnect between policy intent and outcomes.
He was speaking at the Paryavaran Niti Manthan organised by MRAI in association with NITI Aayog in New Delhi on Monday.
To address these issues, he proposed a unified institutional mechanism. “Such a mechanism would ensure continuity in leadership, faster decision-making, better inter-ministerial coordination, and streamlined compliance processes,” Mehta said, adding that the sector is currently governed by multiple ministries and regulatory bodies, resulting in fragmented oversight and operational inefficiencies.
MRAI is the apex national association, representing the interests of the recycling industry with over 1,800 registered members, including most regional trade and product associations. The industry body comprises over 25,000 small and medium enterprises, which in turn directly and indirectly employ 25 lakh people in the recycling industry.
Also Read
The industry body said that despite India having a strong and forward-looking policy architecture for recycling, the key challenge lies in execution. “India has developed some of the most forward-looking policies in the recycling space. The intent is clear and commendable. However, the real challenge lies in ensuring consistent and effective implementation on the ground,” Mehta said.
MRAI also highlighted the complex nature of the recycling ecosystem, pointing to fragmented supply chains, the integration of informal and formal sectors, fluctuating material flows, and global trade linkages, which require specialised institutional understanding.
On policy tools, the association called for a calibrated approach to Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). While endorsing EPR as an effective mechanism, it cautioned against a one-size-fits-all framework, particularly in high-value, market-driven segments such as non-ferrous metals, where excessive regulatory intervention could disrupt efficient systems. It recommended material-specific EPR frameworks aligned with existing ecosystem efficiencies.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has launched a new EPR portal expected to onboard around 50 lakh members for solid waste management, marking a step towards digitising the sector. “Under the E-Waste Management Rules, 2022, the framework has transitioned from a collection-based to a recycling-based approach, expanding its scope to over 100 categories of electronic equipment,” said Bharat Sharma, Member Secretary, Central Pollution Control Board, while addressing the audience at the same event.
He added that while digital tools are improving transparency, challenges remain in integrating the informal sector, strengthening verification systems, and expanding recycling infrastructure.
From the policy perspective, NITI Aayog emphasised the need to move from policy design to implementation. “Circular economy is a strategic lever for resource efficiency, industrial competitiveness, and climate action,” said Priyavrat Bhatti, Programme Lead at NITI Aayog, noting that scaling the ecosystem will depend on stronger institutional frameworks, stable demand for recycled materials, and effective enforcement.

articles.title: India's New EPR Portal Faces Major Implementation Hurdles
articles.author: Whalesbook
articles.content:
India's Ministry of Environment has launched a unified Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal. This digital platform aims to consolidate compliance for producers, recyclers, and regulators, boosting traceability and India's recycling infrastructure. However, experts are concerned it may not overcome long-standing systemic challenges hindering the country's move towards a circular economy. The portal faces the difficult task of turning policy goals into practical reality.
Digital Push: Centralizing EPR Compliance
The new EPR portal is the government's strategic move to use digital tools for environmental management. By bringing different waste streams together, the ministry plans to simplify compliance for companies that produce, import, or own brands (PIBOs), and for waste handlers. The portal aims to register millions, improving transparency and efficiency in tracking recycling results and certifications. India's EPR rules now cover plastics, e-waste, batteries, and tires, with a growing focus on recycling, aligning with national goals for a circular economy and resource efficiency.
Major Hurdles: Systemic Gaps Remain
However, the portal's success depends heavily on solving long-standing structural problems that have hindered past efforts. Industry groups like the Material Recycling Association of India (MRAI) call for a national authority to tackle widespread inefficiencies and poor coordination between government bodies. Recent reports show declining EPR compliance, especially for e-waste, signaling a significant implementation gap. Experts note weak enforcement, inadequate infrastructure, and the exclusion of the informal waste sector as key obstacles. The portal's real success will depend on fostering actual coordination and effective on-the-ground work, not just digitizing current problems.
Risks and Inclusivity: The Challenges Ahead
More broadly, significant risks threaten the portal's real impact. MRAI has warned that a one-size-fits-all approach might disrupt efficient recycling markets, like those for non-ferrous metals. A large part of India's waste management relies on the informal sector, which has been largely excluded from formal EPR, leading to inefficiencies. The portal risks widening the gap for small businesses (MSMEs) struggling with digital compliance, potentially pushing them into informal work. Concerns also remain about the accuracy of recycling data from past EPR certificates. Without a national authority and a plan to include the informal sector, the portal might just become a paperwork exercise instead of driving real change.
Outlook: Closing the Gap Between Policy and Practice
India's waste management market is expected to grow significantly, potentially exceeding $18 billion by 2031, driven by regulations and technology. The circular economy offers substantial economic benefits. However, achieving this requires more than just policies and digital tools; it needs strong on-the-ground implementation and ecosystem building. The EPR portal's true success will be judged by its ability to ensure accountability, boost recycling, and unite all participants in a national waste management plan.
articles.summary: India's Ministry of Environment has launched a unified Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal. This digital platform aims to consolidate compliance for producers, recyclers, and regulators, boosting traceability and India's recycling infrastructure. However, experts are concerned it may not overcome long-standing systemic challenges hindering the country's move towards a circular economy. The portal faces the difficult task of turning policy goals into practical reality.

articles.title: Circular Design Certified Textile Fiber Systems Market Growth to Accelerate by 2035 Amid Regulatory Push and Consumer Demand for Traceability - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.author: IndexBox
articles.content:
Lenzing AG
TENCEL brand, certified circular wood sourcing
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Circular Design Certified Textile Fiber Systems market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global market for Circular Design Certified Textile Fiber Systems is undergoing a structural transformation, shifting from a niche, compliance-oriented segment to a mainstream value proposition embedded in brand strategy and retail operations. As of 2025, the market is characterized by fragmented brand ownership, with competition intensifying between pioneering sustainability brands, incumbent mass-market players launching certified sub-lines, and sophisticated private-label programs from major retail conglomerates. Consumer demand is bifurcating into two primary need states: a high-engagement, values-driven cohort seeking traceability and impact claims, and a convenience-driven cohort accepting circularity as a baseline quality attribute, driven by brand trust and product performance parity. The route-to-market remains the critical bottleneck, as certified fiber systems require segregated supply chains from source to shelf, making logistics control a primary source of competitive advantage and margin protection. Pricing power is concentrated at the premium tier and within private label, where retailers leverage scale to offer certified products at mainstream price points, commoditizing certification and squeezing margins for undifferentiated mid-tier brands. The regulatory and claims environment is shifting from voluntary certification to mandatory extended producer responsibility (EPR) and eco-design requirements in key markets, transforming certification from a brand differentiator into a cost of market entry and compliance. Geographic roles are crystallizing, with Western Europe and North America as premiumization and regulatory lead markets, Asia-Pacific as the dominant manufacturing and sourcing base with growing domestic premium demand, and emerging economies
The baseline scenario for the Circular Design Certified Textile Fiber Systems market from 2026 to 2035 projects robust growth, underpinned by regulatory tailwinds, corporate sustainability commitments, and technological advancements in recycling and traceability. The market is expected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 12.5% over the forecast period, with the market index reaching 325 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth trajectory is supported by the progressive implementation of extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes in the European Union and similar legislation in North America, which mandate minimum recycled content in textiles and shift the cost of end-of-life management to producers. Concurrently, major apparel and footwear brands are accelerating their transition to circular material sourcing, with many committing to 100% recycled or sustainably sourced fibers by 2030, creating a sustained demand pull for certified fiber systems. On the supply side, investments in chemical recycling infrastructure, particularly for polyester and nylon, are scaling capacity and improving the quality of recycled fibers, enabling higher blending ratios in performance and aesthetic applications. The market is also benefiting from the proliferation of digital traceability platforms, such as blockchain-based certification systems, which enhance transparency and consumer trust. However, the baseline scenario acknowledges persistent challenges, including the high cost of certified fibers relative to virgin alternatives, the complexity of segregated supply chains, and the risk of greenwashing accusations that could undermine consumer confidence. The market is expected to see a bifurcation between premium, high-traceability segments and commoditized cert
The apparel and fashion segment is the largest consumer of Circular Design Certified Textile Fiber Systems, accounting for an estimated 45% of global demand in 2025. This segment is driven by aggressive sustainability commitments from major brands such as H&M, Inditex, Nike, and Adidas, which have set targets to source 100% recycled or sustainably certified fibers by 2030. The demand story is characterized by a shift from niche, high-margin sustainable collections to mainstream integration, with certified fibers increasingly used in core product lines. Key demand-side indicators include the volume of post-consumer textile waste collected and sorted, the capacity of chemical recycling facilities, and the adoption of digital product passports for traceability. Through 2035, the segment will see a bifurcation: premium brands will emphasize traceability and impact claims, while mass-market retailers will leverage private-label certified products to capture volume. The growth is supported by regulatory drivers such as the EU's Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles, which mandates minimum recycled content and eco-design requirements. However, challenges include the higher cost of certified fibers and the need for supply chain segregation to maintain certification integrity. Current trend: Strong growth driven by brand sustainability targets and regulatory mandates for recycled content.
Major trends: Integration of certified fibers into core volume-driving product lines, not just niche collections, Rise of digital product passports and blockchain-based traceability to verify claims, and Brand-led take-back and recycling programs to secure feedstock and enhance circularity narrative.
Representative participants: H&M Group, Inditex, Nike, Inc, Adidas AG, Levi Strauss & Co, and Patagonia, Inc.
The home textiles and furnishings segment represents approximately 20% of the market, driven by sustainability initiatives in the hospitality industry, retail home goods chains, and increasing consumer awareness of circular products. This segment includes bedding, towels, curtains, upholstery, and carpets made from certified recycled or regenerated fibers. The demand story is mechanism-based: hotels and resorts are adopting certified textiles as part of their corporate social responsibility (CSR) programs, while retailers like IKEA have committed to using only recycled or renewable materials by 2030. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from the growing trend of 'circular home' concepts, where consumers seek durable, recyclable products. Key demand-side indicators include the volume of post-consumer textile waste from household collections, the availability of certified fibers for home textile applications, and the adoption of eco-labels. The segment faces challenges related to the durability and aesthetic consistency of recycled fibers, particularly for upholstery and high-end furnishings. However, technological improvements in fiber regeneration are closing the quality gap, enabling broader adoption. Regulatory drivers, such as the EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, will also push for recyclability and recycled content in home textiles. Current trend: Moderate growth supported by hospitality and retail sustainability programs and consumer demand for eco-friendly home pr.
Major trends: Hospitality sector adopting certified textiles for CSR and guest experience differentiation, Retailers like IKEA driving volume through private-label certified home textile lines, and Growing consumer preference for durable, recyclable home products with eco-labels.
Representative participants: IKEA, Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide, West Elm, and Crate & Barrel.
The technical textiles segment accounts for an estimated 15% of the market, encompassing applications such as geotextiles, industrial wipes, filtration media, and protective clothing. This segment is driven by the need for high-performance fibers that also meet sustainability criteria, particularly in regulated industries like automotive, construction, and healthcare. The demand story is mechanism-based: technical textiles require specific mechanical, thermal, or chemical properties, and certified recycled fibers must achieve performance parity with virgin materials. Through 2035, the segment will see growth supported by advancements in chemical recycling that produce high-purity polymers suitable for demanding applications. Key demand-side indicators include the adoption of recycled content in automotive interior components (e.g., seat fabrics, carpets) and the use of certified fibers in nonwoven hygiene products. Regulatory drivers, such as the EU's End-of-Life Vehicles Directive and the Circular Economy Action Plan, are pushing for recycled content in automotive and industrial textiles. However, the segment faces challenges related to the consistency of recycled fiber properties and the need for specialized processing equipment. Major companies in this space include fiber producers like Lenzing and Indorama, which supply certified fibers for technical applications. Current trend: Steady growth driven by performance requirements and sustainability mandates in industrial and protective applications.
Major trends: Chemical recycling advancements enabling high-purity fibers for demanding technical applications, Automotive industry adopting recycled content in interior textiles driven by regulatory mandates, and Growth in nonwoven hygiene products using certified fibers for eco-conscious consumers.
Representative participants: Lenzing AG, Indorama Ventures Public Company Limited, Freudenberg Group, Ahlstrom-Munksjö, and Suominen Corporation.
The automotive interiors segment represents approximately 12% of the market, driven by regulatory requirements and automaker sustainability commitments. This segment includes seat fabrics, carpets, headliners, and interior trim made from certified recycled fibers. The demand story is mechanism-based: the EU's End-of-Life Vehicles Directive and similar regulations in other regions mandate increasing levels of recycled content in new vehicles, while automakers like BMW, Tesla, and Volvo have set ambitious targets for using sustainable materials. Through 2035, the segment will see significant growth as automakers integrate certified fibers into mainstream models, moving beyond luxury or eco-trim levels. Key demand-side indicators include the volume of post-consumer textile waste suitable for automotive applications, the development of fiber-to-fiber recycling for nylon and polyester used in airbags and seatbelts, and the adoption of life-cycle assessment (LCA) tools by automakers. The segment benefits from the long product life cycles in automotive, which create a stable demand for certified fibers. However, challenges include the stringent performance and safety requirements for automotive textiles, which necessitate high-quality recycled fibers. Major companies supplying certified fibers to this segment include Toray, Teijin, and Unifi. Current trend: Strong growth driven by regulatory mandates for recycled content and brand sustainability targets in the automotive sect.
Major trends: Automakers setting public targets for recycled content in interiors, driving volume demand, Development of fiber-to-fiber recycling for automotive-grade nylon and polyester, and Integration of certified fibers into mainstream vehicle models, not just premium trims.
Representative participants: BMW Group, Tesla, Inc, Volvo Car Corporation, Toyota Motor Corporation, and Ford Motor Company.
The sportswear and activewear segment accounts for approximately 8% of the market, but is one of the fastest-growing end-use sectors, driven by the convergence of performance requirements and sustainability demands. This segment includes apparel, footwear, and accessories made from certified recycled polyester, nylon, and bio-based polymers. The demand story is mechanism-based: sportswear brands like Nike, Adidas, and Lululemon have pioneered the use of recycled fibers in high-performance products, such as running shoes and yoga pants, leveraging marketing narratives around circularity and innovation. Through 2035, the segment will see growth supported by the development of bio-based and chemically recycled fibers that offer superior moisture management, stretch, and durability. Key demand-side indicators include the adoption of circular design principles in product development, the launch of take-back programs for worn-out sportswear, and consumer willingness to pay a premium for sustainable activewear. The segment benefits from a highly engaged consumer base that values both performance and environmental impact. However, challenges include the need for consistent fiber quality across large production runs and the risk of greenwashing accusations. Major trends: Brands launching circular product lines with take-back and recycling programs, Development of bio-based polymers for performance sportswear applications, and Consumer demand for transparency and traceability in activewear supply chains.
Representative participants: Nike, Inc, Adidas AG, Lululemon Athletica Inc, Puma SE, and Under Armour, Inc.

articles.title: FICCI study flags gaps in used cooking oil supply for biodiesel sector
articles.author: Dailyhunt
articles.content:
A study commissioned by Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry has highlighted major gaps in the supply of used cooking oil (UCO), raising concerns about its availability for biodiesel production in India.
The report shows that out of 72 registered biodiesel plants, nearly 40 percent do not have any formal link with UCO aggregators. Among the rest, 19 units are connected to just one aggregator, 10 have ties with two, and 14 are linked to between three and eleven aggregators. In addition, 17 biodiesel plants are themselves involved in collecting used cooking oil, The Hindu Businessline reported.
According to the study, this uneven distribution points to a weak collection network. It said a stable system would typically involve multiple aggregators operating in the same area to manage supply changes, seasonal variations, and quality differences. The current structure, it noted, reflects an underdeveloped system rather than an efficient one.
The report, titled "Transitioning the Chemical Industry: Used Cooking Oil as a Renewable Feedstock for Enabling India's Material Transition," has recommended making UCO collection mandatory to improve supply for biodiesel and other uses. However, it added that without clear direction on how the oil should be used, it is likely to continue flowing mainly into biodiesel due to existing policy support.
While stronger enforcement could improve collection, the study warned that without a clear system for allocating UCO across different sectors, its full value may not be realised or could be lost through exports.
Looking at global practices, the study noted that China has strengthened its collection systems to prevent the illegal reuse of waste cooking oil. Despite this, much of the collected oil is still used for biodiesel or exported, with limited use in other industries.
In the United States, used cooking oil-known as "yellow grease"-is collected through strict disposal rules for food businesses. Its use is largely guided by fuel-related incentives that support biodiesel and renewable diesel production.
The study also pointed to India's dependence on imported crude oil, which has become more visible amid global tensions in West Asia. It said increasing the use of domestic resources like used cooking oil could help reduce reliance on imports and improve supply stability for key industries.

Among the rest, 19 units are connected to just one aggregator, 10 have ties with two, and 14 are linked to between three and eleven aggregators.

articles.title: 2026 Fendt Harvest Tour Registration Open for Farms Across North America
articles.author: American Ag Network
articles.content:
A Fendt IDEAL 8T combine cuts a row of corn in Petersburg, Iowa. During the 2025 Harvest Tour, Fendt is traveling across five states and dropping the IDEAL combine onto 11 farms, giving midwestern farmers a chance to experience its unique capabilities. The tour also provides Fendt’s harvesting team with an opportunity to listen directly to farmers and learn more about their ideas for improving their harvesting experiences.
Registration is still open for farmers for Fendt’s 2026 IDEAL Harvest Tour, which offers a behind-the-scenes look at peak harvest season this fall.
U.S. farmers are invited to apply for the chance to have their farm featured as a stop on the tour, highlighting harvest conditions, in-field performance and real farmer stories with the Fendt harvest team. While the 2025 tour traveled across five Midwestern states, U.S. farmers can now apply for a chance to put an Ideal to work in their fields.
The Fendt Harvest Tour captures the long days, unpredictable weather and quiet determination that define harvest, while giving farmers the chance to experience how technology is reshaping what’s possible in the field. At each stop of the tour, Fendt will transport its IDEAL® combine directly onto farmers’ fields, bringing its advanced technology and capabilities straight to their operations. Each stop gives farmers a hands-on opportunity to see how Fendt’s precision engineering is reshaping what’s possible in their own fields, from improved efficiency to smarter harvesting.
Registration closes Saturday, May 30. To learn more or to register, additional details can be found here: https://www.fendt.com/us/

Farmers Invited to Join Fendt IDEAL Harvest Tour 2026 Across the U.S.
Fendt has opened registrations for its 2026 Harvest Tour, inviting farmers across North America to participate in an initiative that showcases real harvesting conditions and modern agricultural innovation. The tour provides a unique opportunity for farmers to engage directly with advanced machinery while sharing their own experiences from the field.
The programme allows selected farms to become featured stops on the tour, where harvesting activities are highlighted in real-time. Farmers can demonstrate their field conditions, operational challenges, and daily realities during the harvest season, offering valuable insights into modern farming practices.
A key highlight of the tour is the use of the Fendt IDEAL combine, which is transported directly to participating farms. This enables farmers to experience the machine’s capabilities firsthand, including its performance, efficiency, and precision during actual harvesting operations.
The tour also serves as a platform for knowledge exchange, allowing Fendt’s harvesting team to interact closely with farmers. Through these interactions, the company gathers feedback and ideas that can help improve future farming technologies and better meet the needs of agricultural communities.
By capturing the realities of harvest season, including long working hours and unpredictable weather conditions, the initiative highlights both the challenges and advancements in agriculture. It also demonstrates how modern technology is transforming traditional farming methods by improving productivity and efficiency.
Overall, the Fendt Harvest Tour reflects a growing focus on innovation and farmer engagement in agriculture. By combining hands-on experience with advanced equipment and real-world insights, the tour aims to support farmers in adopting smarter and more efficient harvesting practices.
